stories.title: Nearly half of people with an ileostomy looked dehydrated in a three-country survey
stories.summary: A preprint survey of people with an ileostomy in the UK, Ireland and Australia found that about a third had a high-output stoma. By self-reported urine colour, 48% were dehydrated. Dehydration symptoms went with eating fewer fruits and vegetables, taking more medicines and facing more barriers to drinking. The paper has not been peer reviewed, and it is not North American data.
stories.whyItMatters: Alcohol, heat and hard training all raise fluid losses, so ask your stoma nurse or IBD team what a safe fluid and electrolyte plan looks like for nights out and workouts. Check your urine colour and ask whether any of your medicines add to the risk.

stories.title: Dutch drug bulletin review of mirikizumab: most people still don't reach remission
stories.summary: A Dutch Geneesmiddelenbulletin review looks at mirikizumab, an IL-23 blocker used in both Crohn's and UC. In Crohn's (VIVID-1), 45.4% on the drug (263 of 579) met the first co-primary endpoint, against 19.6% on placebo. In UC (LUCENT-1), week-12 clinical remission was 24.2% versus 13.3% on placebo. The authors conclude it is a useful addition, but the numbers show many patients still don't reach remission.
stories.whyItMatters: Ask your IBD team what the realistic chance of remission is for each option on the table, and which backup plan applies if the first drug doesn't work. If you drink or smoke, say so, because that can shape which drug is chosen.

stories.title: Chinese expert consensus on IBD lifestyle: no alcohol during flares, and limits even in remission
stories.summary: A Chinese health-education post from 28 September 2026 summarises the Chinese expert consensus on lifestyle management in IBD. Alcohol can weaken the gut lining, change gut bacteria and worsen pain and diarrhoea during active disease. In remission, heavy drinking is linked to more relapses and hospital readmissions. It advises quitting smoking through a hospital cessation clinic and says abstaining is the safest choice. The post is a secondary summary and gives no study numbers of its own, so check the consensus text itself.
stories.whyItMatters: Ask your IBD team whether alcohol is sensible while you are flaring or on your current medicines, and plan a drink-free approach for nights out. If you smoke, ask about a formal cessation clinic.
stories.source: Sohu (health-education post citing the Chinese expert consensus on IBD lifestyle management)

stories.title: Dutch adult IBD guideline: drug-treatment modules updated in September 2026
stories.summary: The Dutch Richtlijnendatabase lists a batch of updated modules dated 3 September 2026. They cover biologicals and JAK inhibitors in UC, biologicals and JAK inhibitors in Crohn's, and drug treatment for both diseases, plus a surveillance module. The listing gives no details of what changed, so the exact consequences for reimbursement or drug order aren't clear from this page.
stories.whyItMatters: Ask your gastroenterologist or IBD nurse whether the updated guideline changes your current drug, the order of therapies, or monitoring. It is also worth asking how it affects what your insurer will cover.

stories.title: Steroid-treated IBD: meta-analysis of 27,716 people finds more bone loss, but a less clear rise in osteoporosis
stories.summary: A meta-analysis of 18 studies and 27,716 participants linked glucocorticoid use in IBD to higher odds of abnormal bone density (odds ratio 2.31). The pooled osteoporosis odds ratio for IBD was 1.62. The authors still conclude there was no significant rise in osteoporosis by strict criteria (T-score of −2.5 or lower), especially in UC, despite a tendency toward lower bone density. The results varied a lot between studies. Steroids can also cause muscle weakness.
stories.whyItMatters: If you take or have taken prednisone, ask whether you need a bone-density scan and vitamin D and calcium checks. Also ask if you can move to a steroid-sparing treatment, because heavy lifting is only as safe as the bones and muscles under it.

stories.title: Supervised exercise trial in active IBD shows no quality-of-life gain, and few could stick with it
stories.summary: The IBD-FITT trial in Denmark randomised 44 adults with active IBD to 12 weeks of moderate exercise or usual care. Mean IBDQ scores at week 12 were 172 with exercise and 164 with usual care, which is not statistically different. Only 11 of 22 attended more than half of the sessions, mostly because of scheduling clashes with work. The trial was small, so it can't rule out a benefit.
stories.whyItMatters: Training is not a substitute for medication when your disease is active. Choose a routine you can keep up, and ask the care team or a physiotherapist how hard to push during a flare, especially with fatigue, anaemia or steroid use.

stories.title: Japan UC survey: alcohol is a commonly feared relapse trigger, but lifestyle restrictions did not cut relapse
stories.summary: A Japanese survey of 911 people with ulcerative colitis and 70 clinicians at five academic hospitals found that patients most often named fatty foods (60%), spicy foods (45%) and alcohol (42%) as triggers. About 63% avoided certain foods or drinks, and 47% avoided work, study or housework. Restrictions were linked to worse quality of life but not to fewer relapses, which an April 2026 editorial in Intestinal Research highlighted. The data are self-reported, so alcohol's real effect on relapse remains unproven.
stories.whyItMatters: Strict self-imposed rules can hurt your quality of life without clearly preventing relapse. Ask your care team which restrictions are worth keeping for you, and whether your medicines interact with alcohol.
stories.source: Intestinal Research (editorial on Yamazaki et al.)

stories.title: Lifting and sport with a stoma: feasible, but the evidence is thin and fear of hernia keeps many inactive
stories.summary: A 2026 narrative review pooled guidelines and studies on exercise after ostomy surgery. Tailored activity may improve quality of life, fatigue and fitness. Many people stay inactive because they fear a parastomal hernia, dislike their body image or feel low. Common advice is graded core training, avoiding sudden spikes in abdominal pressure, planning hydration for an ileostomy, and protecting the stoma in contact sports. The authors say there are few randomised trials. The exact publication day was not shown, so the date is approximate.
stories.whyItMatters: Before starting heavy lifting, ask your surgeon or stoma nurse about a staged return to training and whether a support belt suits you. Learn the early signs of a hernia, such as a new bulge or pain around the stoma.

stories.title: ACG 2026 abstract: IBD patients with fatty liver disease before starting a biologic were more likely to have treatment failure
stories.summary: A study highlighted by the American College of Gastroenterology as a newsworthy abstract found that people with IBD who already had metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) before starting a biologic were more likely to see that treatment fail. The summary page I could read did not give the full numbers. It is an observational finding, so it shows an association and not cause and effect.
stories.whyItMatters: If you have a fatty liver diagnosis or drink regularly, ask your GI team whether your liver tests and alcohol intake should be reviewed before or during biologic therapy. Do not stop or switch a biologic on your own because of this early finding.
stories.source: American College of Gastroenterology (ACG 2026 Newsworthy Abstracts)

stories.title: FDA's latest safety-signal list flags possible colitis with three CDK4/6 breast-cancer pills
stories.summary: On Sept. 30, 2026 the FDA posted its quarterly list of potential safety signals, covering reports from April to June 2026. It names colitis as a possible risk with Ibrance, Kisqali and Verzenio. A signal is not a confirmed cause: the FDA says it is evaluating whether regulatory action is needed, and it has not said how many reports it received.
stories.whyItMatters: If you have IBD and are ever prescribed one of these cancer drugs, tell both your oncology and GI teams, and agree in advance on which new bowel symptoms to report. Do not stop a cancer drug without medical advice.
stories.source: CURE Today (reporting on the FDA quarterly signal list)

stories.title: Meta-analysis: soft drinks linked to higher IBD risk, alcohol and coffee to lower risk, but the evidence is weak
stories.summary: A pooled analysis of 27 mostly case-control studies from 16 regions found soft-drink intake linked to a higher risk of developing IBD (OR 1.144). Alcohol (OR 0.793, borderline significance), coffee (OR 0.807) and tea (OR 0.711) were linked to lower risk. The authors say the studies were highly heterogeneous and mostly case-control, so prospective confirmation is needed. This is about who develops IBD, not about how drinking affects people who already have Crohn's or UC. It should not be read as a green light for a night out.
stories.whyItMatters: Don't treat the 'protective' alcohol signal as advice to drink. It is weak observational data on getting IBD, not on flares. Ask your IBD team how alcohol fits with your own medicines and disease activity, and note that sugary mixers and soft drinks were the one clearly unfavourable signal.

stories.title: Meta-analysis of 111,940 IBD patients: smoking history, active disease and high CRP raise the odds of anaemia
stories.summary: A Chinese systematic review pooled 14 studies covering 111,940 people with IBD. It found six risk factors for anaemia. They were older age (OR 1.07), smoking history (OR 1.88), active disease (OR 2.11), and raised CRP (OR about 2.2 in UC and 2.1 in Crohn's). Low albumin was also linked to anaemia, as was penetrating Crohn's behaviour. The data are observational, so the links are associations.
stories.whyItMatters: If you feel unusually wiped out in the gym or on the dance floor, ask for a blood count and iron studies, including ferritin and transferrin saturation. Don't assume it's just poor training or a hangover.

stories.title: Global meta-analysis: about 1 in 3 people with IBD are anaemic, mostly from iron deficiency
stories.summary: A meta-analysis (2015–2024 data) of 138,577 IBD patients from 22 countries estimated anaemia prevalence at 36.9%, with iron-deficiency anaemia at 32.2% and anaemia of chronic disease at 8.1%. In Crohn's disease alone, prevalence was 39.3%. The review points to gaps in monitoring and treatment. The authors are based in India.
stories.whyItMatters: Low iron can cause fatigue, breathlessness and poor workout recovery. Ask how often your iron and haemoglobin are checked, and whether oral or intravenous iron suits your disease activity.

stories.title: Johnson & Johnson's two-drug IBD combination misses its main goal in phase 2b trials
stories.summary: J&J's JNJ-4804 combines golimumab and guselkumab. It was tested in two phase 2b trials, with 693 Crohn's patients and 572 ulcerative colitis patients who had already failed one or more drug classes. The combination did better than either drug alone, but it did not meet the primary endpoint of clinical remission. The company still plans late-stage testing in a subgroup of patients.
stories.whyItMatters: This is a reminder that newer combinations are not yet proven options for people who have failed several advanced drugs. Ask your GI team about trial eligibility and about your optimised options, such as drug-level monitoring.

stories.title: Guselkumab (Tremfya) three-year Crohn's data from the GALAXI 2 and 3 phase 3 trials
stories.summary: On 12 October 2026 Johnson & Johnson announced three-year results from the phase 3 GALAXI 2 and 3 trials of guselkumab in adults with moderately to severely active Crohn's disease. The company says the data show sustained effectiveness and safety. The report I found gave no specific rates, and the data come from the company rather than an independent analysis.
stories.whyItMatters: Long-term follow-up speaks to whether benefit from an IL-23 drug lasts beyond the first year. Company-reported results should be read alongside independent peer-reviewed data.

stories.title: Japanese team builds an MRI score to predict which Crohn's strictures persist after treatment
stories.summary: Institute of Science Tokyo researchers developed and temporally validated a framework using baseline MR enterography. It combines inflammatory activity with structural severity to estimate whether a Crohn's stricture will fail to improve after advanced therapy. The announcement gives no performance figures in the text I could see.
stories.whyItMatters: Strictures can lead to obstruction and surgery, and it is hard to tell early which ones will respond to drugs. If confirmed in other centres, imaging like this could help guide discussions about drug therapy versus earlier procedures.

stories.title: FUZION phase 3: guselkumab perianal fistula remission holds across subgroups, including prior biologic users
stories.summary: New prespecified subgroup analyses of the FUZION trial in Crohn's perianal fistula were presented at ACG 2026. In the overall trial, 28% (100 mg every 8 weeks) and 27% (200 mg every 4 weeks) reached combined fistula remission at week 24, versus 10% on placebo. The company says the results were consistent in subgroups, including people with prior biologic exposure.
stories.whyItMatters: Perianal fistulas are painful, often need surgery, and have had few randomised-trial options. Most patients in FUZION still did not reach combined remission at week 24, so benefit is partial.

stories.title: Anti-TL1A duvakitug: phase 2b RELIEVE UCCD trial published in Lancet Gastroenterology & Hepatology
stories.summary: In the phase 2b trial, adults with moderate-to-severe ulcerative colitis got a 2,250 mg subcutaneous loading dose, then 450 mg or 900 mg every two weeks, or placebo. The primary endpoint was clinical remission at week 14 (modified Mayo score). The analysis covered 137 patients. Medical news coverage reports improved clinical remission in UC and endoscopic response in Crohn's, with no new safety signals and tolerability comparable to placebo.
stories.whyItMatters: Anti-TL1A drugs are a new class that may also affect fibrosis. This is still phase 2b with a 14-week induction period, so longer-term safety and efficacy are unproven.
stories.source: Medical Dialogues, reporting on The Lancet Gastroenterology & Hepatology

stories.title: Brazil: IBD cases rose more than fivefold from 2012 to 2025, a national study finds
stories.summary: A study of Brazil's public health system records, presented at the 74th Brazilian Congress of Coloproctology, found IBD prevalence rose from 30 to 158 cases per 100,000 people between 2012 and 2025. Yearly new diagnoses rose from 9.35 to 12.34 per 100,000. The authors project that new cases could reach 22.7 per 100,000 and prevalence 264 per 100,000 by 2035.
stories.whyItMatters: The rising caseload suggests growing demand for IBD specialist care, monitoring and advanced therapies in Brazil's public system. These are registry figures, not clinical trial results.
stories.source: Prensa Latina (reporting a study presented at the Brazilian Congress of Coloproctology)

stories.title: German-Austrian registry: exclusive enteral nutrition linked to better weight and BMI gains in children with IBD
stories.summary: The CEDATA-GPGE registry analysis covered 450 children (303 Crohn's, 147 UC) followed for four years. Weight and BMI scores rose significantly, and exclusive enteral nutrition was linked to larger gains (BMI SDS +0.67 vs +0.36 without it). Height improved only slightly overall, and the effect sizes were small.
stories.whyItMatters: Poor growth and low weight are common problems in paediatric IBD. These observational data support nutritional therapy as one way to help, and the authors say children with severe or recurrent flares need close monitoring.
stories.source: Hospital Healthcare (reporting a Journal of Pediatric Gastroenterology and Nutrition study)

stories.title: Study: plant-food oxalate may build up in IBD and worsen gut inflammation
stories.summary: A Dutch-language news report describes an August 2026 study in Cellular and Molecular Gastroenterology and Hepatology. It found that in IBD the gut may be less efficient at clearing oxalate, a compound found in some plant foods. The build-up could then make intestinal inflammation worse. The report gave no trial numbers, and I could not confirm the study design.
stories.whyItMatters: It suggests a mechanism by which some commonly 'healthy' foods might matter in IBD. It is not evidence that anyone should change their diet, and food choices are best discussed with an IBD dietitian.
stories.source: Futura-Sciences (NL), on a study in Cellular and Molecular Gastroenterology and Hepatology

stories.title: REMEASURE RCT: Kono-S anastomosis and mesenteric resection gave similar results after first Crohn's ileocolic resection
stories.summary: In this randomized trial, 73 patients with primary ileocolic Crohn's disease had either a Kono-S anastomosis or resection of the mesentery. At six months, endoscopic recurrence was 33% (12/36) with Kono-S and 32% (12/37) with mesenteric resection. Surgical recurrence occurred in only two patients, one in each group. The authors found no significant advantage for either technique in complications or recurrence.
stories.whyItMatters: Neither of two bowel-sparing approaches meant to cut recurrence did better in this trial, so surgical technique alone may not prevent early post-operative recurrence. Post-operative drug therapy and endoscopic follow-up still matter. The authors also reported that adjuvant biologic therapy was protective.

stories.title: New IBD guidance round-up: ECCO on UC drug treatment and infections, ASCRS on UC surgery, AGA on C. diff
stories.summary: A Guideline Central round-up (12 October 2026) lists guidance published since December 2025. It includes ECCO's infections guideline and nursing-roles guidance (July 2026), ECCO's UC medical-treatment guideline (7 July), ASCRS's surgical management of UC (21 May) and AGA's C. difficile in IBD update (May 2026). The AGA update says to test people with IBD who have new or worsening diarrhea, and it favors fidaxomicin or vancomycin for treatment.
stories.whyItMatters: These documents shape how clinics approach infection screening, UC drug choice, UC surgery and diarrhea that flares after C. diff. People with IBD can ask their IBD team how the updates apply to their care.

stories.title: PANCCO publishes evidence-based Crohn's disease guideline for Latin American adults, with 52 recommendations
stories.summary: PANCCO's guideline adapts and updates the 2020 Colombian guideline, following PAHO/WHO methods and GRADE. It updated four of seven clinical questions with searches from January 2020 to February 2026. It makes 52 recommendations covering relapse prediction, conventional and advanced therapy, perianal fistulizing disease, surgery, therapeutic endoscopy and prevention of post-surgical recurrence.
stories.whyItMatters: This is a regional reference for Crohn's care, built around the resources and needs of Latin American health systems. It supports individualized decisions and a multidisciplinary approach.
stories.source: NetMD (summary of PANCCO guideline published in Revista de Gastroenterología del Perú)

stories.title: Fertility treatment often works in women with IBD, ACG 2026 study finds
stories.summary: In a prospective study of women with IBD, 73% of those who had intrauterine insemination (IUI) and/or embryo transfer (ET) became pregnant. Of 67 women, 52 tried to conceive, making 97 attempts (49 IUI, 48 ET). ET worked far better than IUI alone. Neither active disease nor earlier IBD surgery was significantly linked to the results.
stories.whyItMatters: This suggests IBD alone should not rule out assisted reproduction, though the sample was small. Anyone planning a pregnancy would still need to plan with their own care team.

stories.title: PANCCO issues its first Latin American consensus on biosimilars in IBD
stories.summary: The Pan American Crohn's and Colitis Organisation (PANCCO) published a consensus on biosimilars in a Mexican gastroenterology journal. It suggests using infliximab or adalimumab, original or biosimilar, to induce response and remission in Crohn's and in moderate-to-severe UC. It notes that newer therapies are costly and many public systems don't cover them. It cites a systematic review of at least 28 studies and 2,517 patients who switched from an original antibody to a biosimilar.
stories.whyItMatters: Biosimilars may widen access to anti-TNF treatment where costs limit care. The consensus reflects expert agreement on evidence, not a new trial.

stories.title: ACG 2026 symposium: intestinal ultrasound as a bedside tool for guiding IBD care
stories.summary: A symposium on Oct 14 at ACG described intestinal ultrasound (IUS) as a real-time, noninvasive way to see bowel wall layers and track active inflammation without colonoscopy. The speaker said he would use IUS to map the ileum before switching biologics in a patient with ileocolonic Crohn's. He also said showing the images live helps patients understand their disease and how treatment is working.
stories.whyItMatters: IUS may let some people have fewer colonoscopies and get quicker feedback on whether a therapy is working. Access still varies by center, and this report is an expert symposium rather than new trial data.

stories.title: UK IBD-BOOST trial: online self-management for pain, fatigue and urgency did not significantly improve quality of life
stories.summary: The NIHR-funded IBD-BOOST randomised trial tested a 12-session online cognitive-behavioural programme with facilitator support against usual care in people with IBD who had pain, fatigue or urgency/incontinence. It did not significantly improve disease-specific quality of life or global symptom relief at 6 months, though trends favoured the programme. A companion cost-effectiveness analysis was published in BMJ Open Gastroenterology in July 2026.
stories.whyItMatters: This is a negative result for a digital programme aimed at persistent symptoms such as fatigue, pain and urgency. Remission does not remove these symptoms, and non-drug approaches still need better evidence.
stories.source: NIHR (Southampton), via PubMed; BMJ Open Gastroenterology

stories.title: Sprint-interval cardio added to lifting shows no strength penalty versus lifting alone in new meta-analysis
stories.summary: This meta-analysis compared lifting plus sprint interval training with lifting alone in healthy adults. It found no significant differences in lower-body strength (SMD 0.01), upper-body strength (SMD -0.06), jump performance or sprint performance. The excerpt I could see did not give a clear hypertrophy result, and the paper appears to say hypertrophy data are too sparse to conclude.
stories.whyItMatters: Short, hard sprint intervals do not appear to blunt strength gains from lifting, so a hard gainer who wants some conditioning has an option besides long steady cardio. Muscle size was not clearly settled, so keep cardio volume modest and keep eating in a surplus.

stories.title: Meta-analysis of exclusive enteral nutrition in adult Crohn's disease: about 66% remission in real-world studies, but steroids worked better in RCTs
stories.summary: This Indian Journal of Gastroenterology meta-analysis pooled 40 studies with 2,459 adults. The pooled clinical remission rate with EEN was 66% across 23 real-world cohorts (n=1,269). In five RCTs (n=315), corticosteroids beat EEN for remission (RR 0.65). Elemental and non-elemental formulas did not differ in efficacy (RR 1.04).
stories.whyItMatters: Formula-only feeding can help settle active Crohn's in adults, and cheaper non-elemental formulas appear to work as well as elemental ones. It is not better than steroids, and the outcome measured is remission rather than weight or muscle gain. Gaining weight with Crohn's usually depends on controlling the disease first.

stories.title: Systematic review: exercise for bone density in IBD rests on just two RCTs, both in Crohn's disease
stories.summary: Only two randomised trials (164 participants in total) met the criteria, and both enrolled adults with Crohn's disease. Six months of combined impact and resistance training gave higher lumbar-spine bone density than usual care. Hip results were not consistently better, and no randomised evidence existed for ulcerative colitis.
stories.whyItMatters: Supervised lifting with impact work looks feasible in stable Crohn's disease and may protect bone, which matters for a thin person with IBD. The evidence base is small and silent on ulcerative colitis. The review looks at bone, not muscle gain.

stories.title: Umbrella review of 17 meta-analyses: combining lifting and endurance work keeps hypertrophy comparable to lifting alone
stories.summary: The review pooled 17 meta-analyses covering 144 studies and 1,492 healthy participants. Compared with lifting alone, concurrent training gave comparable strength, power and hypertrophy, plus better aerobic capacity (SMD 0.77). Doing lifting before endurance work showed non-significant trends favouring strength and hypertrophy, and elite-athlete data were scarce.
stories.whyItMatters: Moderate cardio for heart health or appetite should not wreck muscle gain in recreational lifters. Put the lifting first in a session and don't let cardio eat into the energy surplus.

stories.title: Brazilian health press: total daily protein matters most, and big single doses may also work
stories.summary: A Brazilian news piece quotes a nutritionist who says total daily protein, at 1.6–2.2 g/kg, is the deciding factor for muscle gain. For a 60 kg person that is about 96–132 g a day. She cites research suggesting single doses of 70–100 g can still support muscle protein synthesis, so the old 20–30 g per meal ceiling may be too strict. She still advises spreading intake over 3–4 meals. This is secondary news coverage that refers to a 2023 study. It is not new trial data.
stories.whyItMatters: If you struggle to eat, you don't have to hit a strict 20–30 g protein cap at every meal. Reaching your daily total (about 1.6–2.2 g/kg) matters more, and larger servings at the meals you can manage are fine.

stories.title: Active ulcerative colitis: new Asian sarcopenia criteria flag more young men with muscle loss
stories.summary: Researchers at Peking Union Medical College Hospital compared 57 hospitalized adults with active UC against 35 healthy controls. They used bioimpedance and handgrip strength and applied the AWGS 2025 sarcopenia consensus. The newer criteria identified 11 more male patients as sarcopenic than AWGS 2019 did. Prevalence in patients aged 18–49 was also significantly higher under the 2025 criteria, and sarcopenic patients had higher hsCRP (p=0.011). The study is cross-sectional and small, and it also looked at gut microbiota and serum metabolites.
stories.whyItMatters: A young person with UC can look fine on BMI and still be under-muscled by current Asian criteria. A grip-strength or body-composition check is worth asking for if you are thin with active disease. This study describes the problem but did not test any treatment.

stories.title: Nutrients review: how to approach malnutrition and oral nutrition therapy in adults with IBD
stories.summary: This narrative review says malnutrition can affect up to 85% of people with IBD. It lays out oral nutritional supplement (ONS) choices by disease stage. In active disease it suggests high-calorie, high-protein formulas at 1.2–1.5 g/kg/day, with easier-to-absorb fats and lactose-free, low-fibre options. For people at risk around surgery, it suggests high-protein ONS for at least 7 days, with at least 18 g of protein per dose, taken 2–3 times a day. ESPEN guidance treats ONS as a first step that supports normal food. This is a review, not a new trial.
stories.whyItMatters: If you have IBD and can't gain weight, ONS fits into a stepwise plan alongside food and is not a replacement for it. Ask your care team or dietitian about formulas suited to your disease stage.

stories.title: Preoperative exclusive enteral nutrition lowered an inflammation-nutrition marker in Crohn's disease but did not change BMI
stories.summary: A Frontiers in Nutrition paper reports that exclusive enteral nutrition (EEN) before surgery improved the CRP-to-albumin ratio in Crohn's disease. The title states this happened without affecting body mass index. The abstract was not available in the search result, so sample size and design are not confirmed here.
stories.region: Asia-Pacific (country not confirmed from the page)
stories.whyItMatters: This is a null result for weight. A short preoperative course of formula feeding can improve inflammation and nutrition markers without raising BMI. It should not be treated as a way to gain weight or muscle, and weight-gain goals may need a separate plan.

stories.title: Whey protein is optional for muscle gain, Brazilian science-communication piece says
stories.summary: The article says controlled trials found that adding whey to an already balanced diet gave only a modest extra gain of about 400–500 g of lean mass. It also says the 'anabolic window' idea of drinking whey right after training has been discarded. It attributes the findings to University of São Paulo researchers but names no specific trial. It says whey is most useful for people with absorption limits, strict calorie restriction or high metabolic needs.
stories.whyItMatters: A hard gainer who already eats enough protein and calories should not expect a protein shake alone to add much muscle. Whey is best used as an easy way to add calories and protein when food intake falls short.

stories.title: Meta-analysis: 'advanced' lifting techniques (drop sets, rest-pause and similar) give only a small edge over standard multi-set training
stories.summary: The review pooled 23 studies in recreationally trained adults aged 18–45. It compared advanced systems with traditional multiple-set programs. When all outcomes were pooled, the advantage was small but statistically significant (g = 0.159). The review also examined whether volume matching and proximity to failure changed the result.
stories.whyItMatters: Fancy techniques are unlikely to be what separates a hard gainer from a good result. Consistent progressive training with enough total volume and enough food matters far more, and drop sets or rest-pause can be an optional extra.
stories.source: Journal of Functional Morphology and Kinesiology (via PubMed)

stories.title: USADA advisory: ostarine (a SARM) keeps turning up as an undeclared ingredient in supplements
stories.summary: USADA reports that some manufacturers illegally add ostarine and other SARMs to supplements, sometimes leaving it off the label or using misleading names. As of April 2026 it had announced 73 cases involving ostarine. As of July 2026 it listed over 80 products containing ostarine on its High Risk List. I viewed the page through a translation link, so the exact publication date is not shown. The July 2026 figure suggests the page was updated in or after July 2026.
stories.whyItMatters: Muscle-building products marketed to thin lifters are a common route for hidden SARMs. Choose third-party-tested products and avoid anything labelled 'research chemical' or 'for research purposes'.
stories.date: July 2026 or later (exact date not shown

stories.title: Sarcopenia in Crohn's disease: borderline predictor of a worse course in a retrospective study
stories.summary: A retrospective observational study modelled which factors predict an unfavourable Crohn's disease course. Disease behaviour (OR about 10.3) and calprotectin above 129 μg/g (OR about 8.5) were significant. Sarcopenia had an OR of about 4.9 but narrowly missed significance (p=0.054, wide CI 0.97–24.3).
stories.whyItMatters: Low muscle mass in Crohn's may flag a harder disease course, but this small retrospective result is not conclusive. If you have Crohn's and struggle to gain, ask for muscle and nutrition assessment as well as inflammation checks.

stories.title: Systematic review: sarcopenia in IBD is linked to worse endoscopic outcomes and loss of biologic response, but evidence is thin
stories.summary: A systematic review with narrative synthesis found sarcopenia and related body-composition measures may be associated with a worse endoscopic course, postoperative recurrence and loss of biologic response. This was seen particularly in Crohn's disease. The authors say the evidence is mostly observational, heterogeneous and based on few studies.
stories.whyItMatters: Building and protecting muscle in IBD is plausibly worthwhile, not just cosmetic. No trial yet shows that gaining muscle improves these disease outcomes.

stories.title: Crossover trial tests whether extra carbohydrate energy improves muscle growth and strength in trained men
stories.summary: A registry record from Auburn University describes a quasi-randomized, double-blinded, counterbalanced crossover trial in 20 resistance-trained men. It tests whether supplemental carbohydrate energy improves hypertrophy, strength and fatigue resistance. The record says the existing evidence on higher energy and carbohydrate intake is mixed. The snippet I found did not include results, so the findings are unconfirmed.
stories.whyItMatters: It targets a core hard-gainer question: whether adding carbohydrate calories on top of training helps muscle gain. Until results appear, treat extra carbohydrate as a way to reach an energy surplus rather than a proven muscle-building aid.

registry.title: This is a Single-center, Prospective, Single-arm Clinical Study Designed to Evaluate the Efficacy and Safety of Oral Aeromonas sp. MTB Phage Therapy for Pouchitis in Patients With Ulcerative Colitis (UC).
registry.officialTitle: A Single-center, Prospective, Single-arm Clinical Research Protocol for the Treatment of Pouchitis With Aeromonas sp. MTB Bacteriophage
registry.summary: The goal of this single-arm, prospective clinical trial is to assess the clinical efficacy and safety of oral Aeromonas sp. MTB-specific phage therapy in adult participants aged 18-70 years with pouchitis following ileal pouch-anal anastomosis (IPAA) for ulcerative colitis, who are positive for stool MTB bacteria or aerolysin. stories.title: Switching children with IBD from IV to subcutaneous infliximab kept most in remission
stories.summary: A meta-analysis pooled six small pediatric cohorts (173 children) that switched from intravenous to subcutaneous infliximab. About 92% stayed on treatment and 93% stayed in clinical remission, while 8% stopped for any reason, mostly due to injection-site problems, relapse, or paradoxical dermatitis. New anti-drug antibodies were rare (four children, none sustained), and drug levels were about 2-fold higher than before the switch.
stories.whyItMatters: It suggests that subcutaneous infliximab, which is not yet approved for people under 18, may be a workable option that cuts school absence and travel for children with IBD, though the evidence comes from observational cohorts and still needs prospective confirmation.
stories.originalTitle: Switching from Intravenous to Subcutaneous Infliximab in Children with Inflammatory Bowel Disease: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis

stories.title: Tofacitinib 20 mg and 30 mg worked similarly in acute severe ulcerative colitis
stories.summary: In a small double-blind pilot trial of 72 adults with acute severe UC, all received IV corticosteroids plus tofacitinib at 20 or 30 mg/day. Clinical response at day 7 was 91.7% with 20 mg and 86.1% with 30 mg, a difference that was not statistically significant. Rescue therapy, treatment escalation or colectomy within 90 days was similar (event-free survival 83.3% vs 80.2%), and adverse events were mostly mild with no blood clots or major cardiovascular events reported.
stories.whyItMatters: This early evidence suggests that a higher tofacitinib dose may not add benefit over the lower dose in hospitalized severe UC, though the trial was too small to be conclusive.
stories.originalTitle: Tofacitinib 20 vs 30 mg in acute severe ulcerative colitis: a double-blind randomized controlled trial

stories.title: Machine learning shows promise for predicting anti-TNF response in Crohn's, especially with imaging data
stories.summary: A meta-analysis of 29 studies with 6,697 Crohn's patients assessed machine learning models that predict response to anti-TNF therapy. In external validation, models using radiomic (imaging) features scored a C-index of 0.865, and models combining clinical and radiomic features scored 0.883. Models using clinical features alone scored 0.733. The authors noted methodological limitations.
stories.whyItMatters: In the future, such tools might help identify early who is unlikely to respond to anti-TNF drugs, but they need more validation across diverse groups of patients before routine use.
stories.originalTitle: The predictive value of machine learning for the response to anti-TNF-α therapy in patients with Crohn's disease: a systematic review and meta-analysis

stories.title: Oral icotrokinra pill beat placebo for response in moderate-to-severe ulcerative colitis
stories.summary: In a phase 2b randomized trial of 252 adults with moderately to severely active UC, clinical response at week 12 was 63%, 58% and 55% with 400, 200 and 100 mg daily icotrokinra, versus 27% with placebo. At 400 mg, clinical remission was 30% vs 11% and endoscopic improvement was 37% vs 14%. Adverse events were similar across groups through week 28 (60-66%).
stories.whyItMatters: It suggests a once-daily pill that blocks the interleukin-23 pathway could one day be an alternative to injected or infused IL-23 antibodies, though larger and longer trials are needed.
stories.source: The New England journal of medicine
stories.originalTitle: Phase 2 Trial of Icotrokinra for Patients with Ulcerative Colitis

stories.title: Etrasimod lowers inflammatory immune cells in blood and gut lining in UC
stories.summary: Using blood from 782 and gut biopsies from 611 patients in the phase 3 ELEVATE UC trials, etrasimod reduced circulating T- and B-cell subsets at week 12 compared with placebo. Gut tissue showed fewer T cells, B cells, myeloid cells and neutrophils, with reduced IL-17 and IL-8 signaling. Changes consistent with tissue repair were most prominent in patients who reached remission.
stories.whyItMatters: It helps explain how this oral UC medication works on the immune system and the gut lining.
stories.originalTitle: Etrasimod reduces circulating and mucosal inflammatory lymphocyte populations and alters innate immune and non-immune cell signatures in intestinal mucosa: ELEVATE UC phase 3 clinical data

stories.title: Fast-recovery surgery pathways shorten hospital stays for people with IBD
stories.summary: A meta-analysis of 18 studies (one randomized trial, 17 observational) found enhanced recovery protocols cut hospital stay by about 1.6 days (moderate certainty). There were no clear differences in 30-day readmissions, reoperations or complications, though certainty for these was low to very low.
stories.whyItMatters: If you need bowel surgery, enhanced recovery programs may mean a shorter hospital stay without evidence of more readmissions or complications, though the evidence is mostly observational.
stories.source: Colorectal disease : the official journal of the Association of Coloproctology of Great Britain and Ireland
stories.originalTitle: Enhanced recovery after colorectal surgery in patients with inflammatory bowel disease to reduce hospital length of stay: A systematic review and meta-analysis

stories.title: Stem cell therapy closed about 6 in 10 Crohn's perianal fistulas long-term
stories.summary: A meta-analysis of 18 studies with 750 patients and 12 months to 4 years of follow-up found a pooled long-term healing rate of 59% in randomized trials and 63% across all designs. No treatment-related deaths or clear therapy-linked cancers were found.
stories.whyItMatters: It suggests stem cell treatment may give lasting healing for fistulas that haven't responded to standard care, although study designs differ.
stories.source: Colorectal disease : the official journal of the Association of Coloproctology of Great Britain and Ireland
stories.originalTitle: Long-term clinical outcomes of stem cell-based interventions in Crohn's-related perianal fistula: A systematic review and meta-analysis

stories.title: Under-the-skin infliximab kept most children with IBD in remission after switching
stories.summary: A pooled analysis of five cohorts (162 children, mostly Crohn's) found treatment persistence of about 90% and clinical remission of about 90% at roughly 6 months. Infliximab blood levels roughly doubled after the switch, new antidrug antibodies were rare (0.7%), and injection site reactions occurred in 11%. Certainty was low to very low, and nearly all children switched while already in remission.
stories.whyItMatters: It offers early reassurance for families considering a switch from intravenous to subcutaneous infliximab, which is currently off-label in children, but it does not show the injection can start treatment.
stories.originalTitle: Subcutaneous infliximab for maintenance therapy in children and adolescents with inflammatory bowel disease: a systematic review and meta-analysis

stories.title: Trial testing a phone-based CBT program for fatigue in IBD remission is under way
stories.summary: This is a protocol for an open-label, waitlist-controlled randomized trial of a 7-week app-based cognitive behavioral program for fatigue in people with IBD in remission. 351 patients were randomized; 151 of 502 screened were excluded for having little fatigue (FACIT-F of 40 or higher). No results are available yet and are expected in 2027.
stories.whyItMatters: Fatigue is common even in remission, and this trial could show whether a scalable app-based approach helps, but there are no findings yet.
stories.originalTitle: Evaluation of a Mental Health Care App-Based Fatigue Management Program for Patients With Inflammatory Bowel Disease in Remission: Protocol for a Randomized Controlled Trial

stories.title: COVID-19 didn't worsen IBD course, but interrupted biologics raised flare risk
stories.summary: Across four matched cohorts (about 1,300 patients), prior COVID-19 was not linked to worse IBD course (OR 1.06; 95% CI 0.76-1.49). COVID-19 was linked to delayed or stopped biologics (OR 10.44), and flares were more frequent when biologics were delayed or stopped (about 52% vs 18%).
stories.whyItMatters: It suggests the bigger concern after COVID-19 may be interrupted IBD treatment rather than the infection itself, though the evidence is limited to a few observational cohorts.
stories.originalTitle: COVID-19 AND IBD: LOOK BEYOND THE VIRUS. A SYSTEMATIC REVIEW AND META-ANALYSIS FOCUSED ON BIOLOGIC THERAPY CONTINUITY

stories.title: Neutrophil traps are high in IBD and blocking them eased colitis in animal models
stories.summary: A review of 48 studies found markers of neutrophil extracellular traps were raised in the gut and blood of people with IBD and linked to more severe disease and poorer prognosis. In animal models, blocking or breaking down these traps reduced disease activity and tissue damage and improved gut barrier function. Several results were not robust in sensitivity analyses.
stories.whyItMatters: This is early-stage science pointing to a possible future treatment target, with no human treatment trials yet.
stories.originalTitle: Neutrophil extracellular traps as a potential therapeutic target in inflammatory bowel disease: a systematic review and meta-analysis

stories.title: Stem cells and anti-TNF drugs both help Crohn's fistulas; no clear winner
stories.summary: A network meta-analysis of 15 randomized trials (2,475 patients) found stem cells improved fistula remission (OR 5.33) and response (OR 4.76) versus placebo. Anti-TNF drugs also improved fistula remission (OR 2.19) and were better for overall clinical remission (OR 2.41). Indirect comparison showed a non-significant trend favoring stem cells for fistula healing, and both had safety similar to placebo.
stories.whyItMatters: Both options appear to work for perianal Crohn's fistulas, but without head-to-head trials it is unclear which is better.
stories.originalTitle: Efficacy and safety of tumor necrosis factor-α inhibitors and mesenchymal stem cells in the treatment of fistulizing Crohn's disease: a systematic review and network meta-analysis

stories.title: Balloon dilation of Crohn's strictures helped avoid surgery over 7 years better than stents
stories.summary: In a long-term follow-up of 80 patients from the ProtDilat trial (median 77 months), 31.5% needed surgery. Balloon dilatation (HR 0.26), a single endoscopic treatment (HR 0.33) and no medical therapy intensification (HR 0.22) were linked to lower surgery risk. Adverse events were less frequent with endoscopic treatment than surgery (8.75% vs 36%).
stories.whyItMatters: It suggests endoscopic balloon dilation can delay or avoid surgery for many people with Crohn's strictures, though this is a retrospective follow-up of an open-label trial.
stories.originalTitle: Self-expandable metal stents versus endoscopic balloon dilatation for the treatment of strictures in Crohn's disease: a retrospective long-term follow-up of the ProtDilat study, an open label, multicenter, randomized trial
